note: Four substantive community-authored language works plus one excluded comparative supporting reference. Actual selected content was inspected. No main/site data, build or publication changed.

proposedParagraphs.title: Language names and relationships
proposedParagraphs.text: Akateko and Awakateko are different Maya languages: the Akateko grammar groups Akateko with Q’anjob’al, Chuj and Popti’, while the Awakateko community’s atlas places Awakateko in the Mamean group and identifies its original core in Aguacatán.

proposedParagraphs.title: Shared writing conventions
proposedParagraphs.text: The Akateko community’s 2024 normative grammar presents writing conventions for teachers, public servants and other readers. Its letter distinguishes standardizing written forms from changing people’s speech and recognizes that rules may be revised. Later examples compare regional pronunciations before specifying written forms. The work offers a substantial guide to community language planning, while proposed conventions remain distinct from a claim that everyone speaks identically or uses the book.

proposedParagraphs.title: Documenting variation through community research
proposedParagraphs.text: The 2013 descriptive revision draws on fieldwork and review workshops in San Miguel Acatán and San Rafael La Independencia. It describes differences between their speech while leaving open precisely how to classify that variation. Its discussions of classifiers and regional vocabulary demonstrate that learning the language involves grammatical relationships and situated usage. The introduction explicitly presents a description of speech at a particular moment. It should not be converted into a timeless catalogue of how every Akateko person speaks.

proposedParagraphs.title: Teaching listening, speaking, reading and writing
proposedParagraphs.text: Kukuy Ti’e Akateko offers teachers a sequence linking listening and speaking with literacy. Its introduction places Akateko culture at the center of learning and connects teachers, students and families. Actual lessons pair written forms with Spanish glosses, pronunciation practice and classroom prompts; later exercises provide space for learners’ written responses. The work documents a developed educational approach. Its aims and preparation credit do not by themselves establish where it is taught today or how learners have experienced it.

proposedParagraphs.title: Place names as community knowledge
proposedParagraphs.text: The 2019 toponymy study treats names as part of Akateko cultural heritage and language continuity. It revises earlier work through local knowledge, combining place descriptions, historical accounts and analysis of meaningful word parts. The conclusion credits older community members as important sources. Reading such entries shows how language and local history meet, while particular explanations remain attributed to the study. Published names and dated settlement descriptions should not be mistaken for current demographic records or an authorization to enter private or culturally sensitive places.

integrationNotes: The 2013 descriptive report and 2024 normative grammar are different works with different aims. They share an institutional and earlier research lineage; do not describe overlapping examples as independent fieldwork corroboration.

Akateko / Akatek / Acateco naming should retain geographical and author context. The comparative Awakateko atlas supplies direct primary support for distinguishing the similar names, rather than assuming they are spelling variants.
Do not infer a single political government or U.S.-style tribe from the Guatemalan term Comunidad Lingüística.
Do not repeat unverified current speaker totals. The 2024 grammar’s demographic statement and its inconsistent 1987 decree citations were excluded from the proposed prose.
The lesson manual credits preparation in 2011. A separate publication date has not been established; do not treat its 2025 upload directory as a new edition.
No cultural stories, ritual instructions, site coordinates, language-recording audio, images, or tables are reproduced. Link to the community’s own works rather than republishing them.
researchGaps: Current community-approved teaching use, learner experiences and outcomes have not been independently established.
Add inspected specialist scholarship by Roberto Zavala when lawful substantive full text is accessible; article metadata and an abstract are not treated as full reading.
Confirm historical name changes through appropriately contextualized sources, rather than projecting present language labels onto all earlier records.
Current demographic claims require the underlying census category, question, date and geographic scope; none is established by this batch.
